title: Shoppers buy the glacier, not the bottle: 58% choose us for the source
subtitle: FY26 survey of 1,500 bottled-water shoppers

items.text: choose the brand for its glacier source above taste or price
is what most will pay for 750 ml, against £1.20 for spring water
would switch to a refillable glass bottle with a deposit
more repeat buying among shoppers who scan the ice-cam code
can name the glacier the water actually comes from

points.text: Nearly three in five buyers name the glacier as their reason, and they pay 65p more than for spring water to get it. The label should lead with the ice, not the price.
One in three would switch to refillable glass, about 4 million bottles a year at today's volumes, and the deposit pays for the washing line.
Shoppers love the glacier but only 12% can name it. The ice-cam code turns a vague idea into a real place, and its scanners buy again 2.4 times as often.

title: Bubbles love a muggy evening: humid air triples their lifespan
subtitle: Average life of a two-metre bubble and what follows, 2026 outdoor tour of 140 shows

items.label: Humidity above 60%
items.text: Giant bubbles last 41 seconds on average against 13 in dry air: long enough to drift over the whole audience and pop above the back row, which is where the cheers are loudest.

items.label: Shows moved to dusk
items.text: Evening slots gain 18 points of humidity on the 3pm ones and sell 2,300 more seats a month at the same venues, because families come after school and dinner.

items.label: Wind under 8 km/h
items.text: Two-metre bubbles reach the back row intact; above that speed they tear within three seconds, so the crew switches to the indoor tent set and loses no performance.

items.label: Glycerine at 6%
items.text: A thicker film adds 9 seconds to every bubble for €0.40 more a show, which a single extra ticket pays back several times over.

items.label: All four at once
items.text: The four-metre cathedral bubble stays up a full minute, so it becomes a nightly finale rather than a lucky one, and it is the clip every audience films.

bar: Book next summer's outdoor tour by the humidity chart, not the calendar: muggy towns at dusk fill first.

title: Five workshop rules keep every wind-up toy ticking past 10,000 turns
subtitle: The rules every toy is built and tested to, from first sketch to final wind

items.title: Brass, never plastic
items.text: Every spring and gear is cut from brass, never moulded plastic, so a toy still walks after 10,000 winds. The brass costs 40p more a toy and saves three returns in every hundred.

items.title: One key fits all
items.text: A single quarter-turn key winds all 64 toys in the range, so a lost key never strands a robot. Spare keys ship in every box and hang by every shop till.

items.title: Thirty seconds a wind
items.text: Each full wind runs for thirty seconds: long enough to cross a kitchen table, short enough to want another go. Longer springs were tested in 2025 and bored the panel.

items.title: Mend, never bin
items.text: Any toy comes back to the bench for free repairs for life, and 96% of them leave walking. Parts from the broken 4% go into the next batch of spare gears.

items.title: Tested by children
items.text: A panel of 40 children under ten signs off every new walk, hop and flip before it ships. A toy needs 30 of the 40 to grin, and only two in five pass first time.

source: Source: Synthetic demonstration • no real company data; the clockwork foreman's notebook

title: Kingston and Havana load half our cargo, and all of it sails via Nassau

sizeLegend.label: Cargo loaded, thousand barrels a year

points.text: Kingston and Havana load 77,000 of 150,000 barrels a year, mostly rum and molasses bound for the northern ports.
Every route calls at Nassau to clear its cargo, so one missed tide there delays ships from all seven ports at once.
Navy patrols off Cartagena add two days to the run north, which is why its sloops now sail only in convoy.
A second berth at Nassau would cut the average wait to unload from three days to one, and pay back in a season.
The planned Veracruz run, dashed, waits on that berth: it would add an eighth port to a hub that is already full.

source: Source: Synthetic demonstration • no real company data; the quartermaster's waterlogged manifest
